meta.description: Rosa Parks did answer the bus driver — but the words she recorded were shorter. Wikiquote lists this longer wording as unsourced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You may go on and do so'?
meta.ogDescription: Right woman, wrong words. Parks’s own account of 1 December 1955 gives her reply as the four-word “You may do that.”

answer.label: Rosa Parks — but not in these words
answer.authorDates: 1913–2005 · Civil rights organiser and seamstress, Montgomery, Alabama
answer.sourceLine: The exchange is real. On 1 December 1955 the driver James F. Blake ↗ told Parks he was going to have her arrested, and she answered him. But the words in her own account are shorter than the version that circulates: “You may do that.” Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ prints the full exchange in that form, while the longer “You may go on and do so” sits in the Unsourced list on its talk page ↗, where an editor notes that her memoir Rosa Parks: My Story gives the four-word reply.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed wording — the moment is real and hers; this phrasing is not the one she recorded.

source.heading: What she recorded saying

docMeta.dd: Cleveland Avenue bus, Montgomery, Alabama, 1 December 1955

docMeta.dt: Status of “You may go on and do so”

source.excerpt: The driver of the bus saw me still sitting there, and he asked was I going to stand up. I said, “No.” He said, “Well, I’m going to have you arrested.” Then I said, “You may do that.”
trail: The sourced wording — Wikiquote’s Rosa Parks entry ↗ carries the exchange with the driver in its quotations section and renders her reply as “You may do that.”

The circulating wording — “You may go on and do so” appears on Wikiquote only in the Unsourced list of Talk:Rosa Parks ↗, alongside an editor’s note citing Rosa Parks: My Story (p. 116) for the shorter reply.

The encounter itself is not in doubt — Wikipedia’s article on James F. Blake ↗ documents the 1 December 1955 confrontation, his order to the four seated passengers and his decision to call the police.

What we could not do — every scanned copy of Rosa Parks: My Story on the Internet Archive ↗ is lending-restricted, so we could not read page 116 ourselves. The page-116 reading here is reported as Wikiquote’s editors give it, not as something we confirmed in the book.
source.excerptNote: The exchange as Wikiquote’s sourced Rosa Parks entry ↗ prints it. Four words, not six — and no “go on”.
source.rightsHolder: The estate of Rosa Parks and her publishers
source.rightsNote: Her account of the arrest was published in Rosa Parks: My Story, written with Jim Haskins. The editions catalogued on the Internet Archive are dated 1994 and 1999, far later than the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff, so the text is firmly in copyright. The four spoken words themselves are far too short to carry a copyright of their own; what is protected is her written telling of them.

author.name: Rosa Parks
author.heading: About Rosa Parks
author.metaLine: 1913–2005 · Civil rights organiser, seamstress and NAACP secretary
author.bio: Rosa Parks had been secretary of the Montgomery NAACP for over a decade before 1 December 1955, and had been put off a bus by the same driver, James Blake, in 1943. Her account of the arrest is notable for how undramatic it is: she describes a short exchange and a flat refusal. The plainness is the point — and it is why the smoother, longer versions of her reply are worth checking.

misattribution.heading: Right woman, wrong words
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is being credited here. The dispute is not about who spoke but about what was said — and the version in circulation is two words longer and a good deal more formal than the one she wrote down.

items.why: Her reply to the driver’s threat is given as “You may do that” in Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ and, per its editors, in her memoir at page 116.

items.who: “You may go on and do so”
items.why: Longer and more stately than the recorded reply. Wikiquote holds it only in the Unsourced list on Talk:Rosa Parks ↗.
Blake did threaten her with arrest and she did answer him; the documented account of the encounter ↗ is consistent on that.

misattribution.truthLine: She said it — in four words. The six-word version is a retelling, and Wikiquote files it as unsourced ↗.

context.heading: Why the wording matters here
lead: This is the smallest kind of error and one of the most instructive. Nobody has stolen the quote, invented a speaker or moved the date — the sentence has simply been smoothed in retelling, from a curt four words into something that scans more like a speech.
The flatness of the real reply is what people who study the moment keep pointing at. She did not make a declaration; she declined, briefly, and let him do what he had said he would do.
detailsBody: Parks had met James Blake before. In 1943 he had made her pay at the front of the bus and then board by the rear door, and drove off while she was walking round — an incident she remembered clearly. On 1 December 1955 he was driving the Cleveland Avenue bus when he told four seated Black passengers to give up their row.

Three of them moved. Parks moved to the window seat and stayed. When Blake said he would have her arrested, she answered, and he called the police. Her arrest that evening set the Montgomery bus boycott in motion within days.
context.pull: Four words, not six — and the shorter one is harder.
